segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Kelsay Irby isn't somebody who likes being in the spotlight-- in fact, kind of the opposite. And she wasn't looking to get in the newspaper the night that she did the thing that got her national attention. She was just showing up to work like normal at the emergency room at a hospital an hour or so outside Seattle, St. Michael's Medical Center.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: So that night when I came in at 7:00, I was looking at the number of patients that were there, which was high.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Like really high. People were all over the lobby in a messy chaos, sitting in wheelchairs because there weren't enough regular chairs, sitting on the floor, sick kids and their parents, ambulance crews with patients waiting to be seen. Kelsay says it was like an airport gate where the flight's just been canceled. A lot of dissatisfaction, a lot of unrest. And she was short-staffed. Kelsay is the charge nurse. So it's her job to make sure all these patients get seen and that she has enough staff to do that, which has been a problem since COVID at hospitals all over the country, hers included.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So many nurses burned out and left the profession since COVID that it's left hospitals perpetually short-staffed, which, Kelsay points out, makes the job that much more stressful for the nurses who stayed and leads to more of them saying that they can't take it, throwing in the towel, making the problem worse. The people who run Kelsay's hospitals say their staffing levels are in line with national standards and best practices. But Kelsay says, typically, she only has half the nurses she should have for the night shift-- half.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: So I was already short-staffed. And then I was going to be two more down. Two of my 7:00 nurses had called in sick.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And if that weren't enough, they'd had a cyberattack. This was a ransomware attack this past October at one of the largest nonprofit hospital chains in the country. CommonSpirit Health, which meant that, suddenly, they couldn't access patients' medical records on the computer for two weeks.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: I cannot overstate how chaotic that made things and how much it slowed us down.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Normally she keeps track of everybody in the lobby by opening their charts in the computer where she can see if they have lab results yet and get the basic information to figure out who can wait longer and who needs care right away.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: And I can see if I need to keep my eye on this patient, or this patient came in for chest pain, but they got punched in the chest by their brother. You know, chances are that it's probably not a heart attack. But because we didn't have our computer system, I wasn't able to see anything other than just "chest pain." Yeah, so--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: And I couldn't see vital signs. I couldn't see labs. I couldn't see anything about the patient's history. That is very much like a pilot, you know, flying without instruments in a foggy, stormy night.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I can't tell as you describe this-- I can't tell, like, is this just a really bad night? Or is this like the worst you'd ever seen?

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: It was the worst I'd ever seen for all of those reasons. I just felt like it had the potential to be a huge catastrophe.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A huge catastrophe means what?

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: The thing that we always worry about the most and the thing that we say a lot when we are short-staffed is we are one bad car accident away from people dying. And not long ago, we had a hospital here in the area who actually had a patient die in the lobby, in the waiting room in the ER.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Actually, the patient, a 41-year-old woman, became unresponsive in the waiting room and then was pronounced dead when she got into an ER bed.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: And that's a huge-- that's a huge fear. I'm just terrified that we're going to go out there and find somebody dead.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She realized she just had to get more nurses to cover these cases. So she did the normal things that a charge nurse is supposed to do in that situation. First, she checked with the hospital supervisor, a.k.a. the house mom.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: I don't know what we'll ever do if it's a guy because the "house mom" is really the term.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The house mom has the power to send somebody from elsewhere in the hospital to help out in the ER for a few hours-- nurses, lab techs who can draw blood, transport staff, anybody. So she reaches the house mom.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: And that night, there was nothing. There was no available help to be had.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Second thing she tries, she asked that they page every single person who works for the ER, see if anybody who's not working will come in. Nobody says yes. Third thing, she asks if they can divert ambulances to other hospitals so they're not adding to the patient count in her emergency room. But she's told, no, computers are down at the hospital they would send patients to and they're struggling also.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Fourth thing, there's an ambulance company that the ER has a contract with and has called in, in the past, in exactly this kind of situation where they're short-staffed.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: To help us take vital signs on patients in the lobby or just do a tour of the lobby and just check on everybody. Those are things that helps us process patients faster.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But the ambulance company was too busy to send anybody. So she tried four things, all the normal things you're supposed to do. Four things failed. Was there any place else she could turn for more help? Then she got an idea, the thing that landed her in the papers. She called 911.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The headlines basically were, ER nurse calls 911 for help. Though, I should say, she did not actually dial the numbers 9 then 1 then 1. She has a regular phone number that you can call and just talk to the 911 dispatcher.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: It wasn't like a momentous decision-making process for me. It was just desperation.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: [BEEP]

segments.speaker: 911 Dispatcher
segments.text: Central communications, how can I help you?

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: Hey, this is Kelsay over at St. Mike's in the ED. I am calling to see if you guys have any available crews that can come in and help us in our lobby. We are drowning.

segments.speaker: 911 Dispatcher
segments.text: OK, hang on for me one moment.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: OK, yeah, I don't know what hoops I have to jump through, but my house mom is drowning as well. So I thought, I'm just going to call and see what I might be able to make happen.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Can I just say the thing that really strikes me is you sound so calm.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: And that is really kind of part of the job description of being the charge nurse. And I've been like that my whole life, even as a kid. In the moment of crisis, I tend to stay pretty calm and focused and get home and cry.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Did you go home and cry at the end of this night?

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: That night and, yeah, though it wasn't the only time that I went home and cried during that week.

segments.speaker: 911 Dispatcher
segments.text: How many patients are there?

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: Right now I have, it looks like, about-- so I have about-- so in the lobby, I have two nurses for about 45 patients, which is horrible.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: And I can hear it in my voice. I can hear my alarm. Even though it sounds to the outsider that I sound like I'm really calm, I can hear little things in my voice that tell me that I'm freaking out, and I'm trying to hide it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah, yeah, tell me what you're hearing that gives that away to you.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: The laughter, really, is the thing that gives that away to me.

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: I mean, I know it's like unprecedented times, unprecedented request, but I figured it was worth a shot.

segments.speaker: 911 Dispatcher
segments.text: Right--

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: A little nervous laugh, kind of like, I don't know what else to do. It's almost like I am-- I'm throwing myself at your mercy because I have no, I have no other options.

segments.speaker: 911 Dispatcher
segments.text: What's your name?

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: Kelsay. I'm a charge nurse tonight. Lucky me.

segments.speaker: 911 Dispatcher
segments.text: OK. OK. Yeah, I'm going to see what we can do here.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: 911 decides to help her out. They sent an ambulance crew with three people. The three of them work the lobby, help monitor and process patients. They're there for nearly two hours, which is enough to get Kelsay over the hump. Afterwards, when nurses around the country hear about this, they call Kelsay a shero, they reach out to her. Some of them said, thanks for the idea, call 911. I'm going to keep that one in mind just in case.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Did it seem heroic to you, what you did?

segments.speaker: Kelsay Irby
segments.text: Not at all. Not at all. I don't see it that way. And I just saw it as solving a problem, doing my job trying to solve a problem.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She was the charge nurse. It was on her to figure things out. She basically raised her hand when she took the job and said, I'm it, and then had to deal with everything that followed, stuff she never predicted or imagined, which is true of everybody in our show today. We have stories where people are like, oh, I'm going to be the one to fix that. And only later did they really discover, to their surprise, what that can really entail. Even when you think you see things coming, you've got it under control, that's who you are, you do not see things coming. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, Every day is Father's Day. Family relationships, they get set in certain patterns that usually just harden over time. I heard somebody recently used the word "cooked" to describe their relationship with a parent. That relationship is cooked, it's done, it's not going to change. Megan Tan felt that way about her and her dad.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: For years, they'd been distant. He was super critical of her. She stopped engaging, moved across the country, stayed away. And then something happened that made Megan decide to try to uncook the relationship, to remake it with different ingredients, which is one of the things that you just can't tell how it's going to go till you try. Here's Megan.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: My relationship with my father has always felt tail-chasing, like we can never get close. It just didn't work. We're pretty different. And he'll be the first to tell you how. This is a call from 2021.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Yes, you're more emotional than--

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Than you are?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: 'Cause you cry out in the open.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I do cry out in the open. [CHUCKLING] What about you? When do you cry? Do you cry ever?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Don't compare. I don't cry. I hardly cry.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Oh, why?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: That's me. That's the way I was brought up.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: "That's the way I was brought up," he says. But it's hard to get him to say more than that. It's conversations like this that remind me I'm always getting to know my father.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: When I was little, he didn't teach us the language he grew up speaking. So I thought one way we could become close is if I learned Mandarin Chinese. When I was a freshman in college, I spent a whole year in the library learning how to write characters, doing rote memorization, burning phrases into my brain.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: [SPEAKING IN MANDARIN]

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: [SPEAKING IN MANDARIN] Happy New Year, that's common thing people [INAUDIBLE].

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Come on, Dad, I'm trying here.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Over the phone, I remind him of what happened my first break home from college. We sat across the table and I showed off my new skills.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I wanted to learn Chinese because I was trying to understand you and trying to get closer to you. And then I studied and studied and studied. And then I came home. That was the first time you ever told me that you didn't speak Chinese.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Yep. Surprise.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: "Surprise," he says. And, yeah, I was surprised, shocked, really. Especially when I said, [SPEAKING IN MANDARIN] and he said, I have no idea what you're saying. I was 18 years old when my dad told me for the first time he spoke Teochew. In the end, he told me I should learn Spanish instead. It's more practical in America.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I suppose this is when I should share some warm childhood memories of my dad. But when I reach back in my memory, I don't really see him. I don't see him at my birthday parties, volleyball games, or academic award ceremonies. He was pretty closed off, icy, shuttered. I remember how he always said "no," how walking around him meant you walked softly. I remember his mood swings and how nothing I did felt like it was enough.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I would tell him I got all A's. He would say, but you didn't do the dishes. I would pay for my own ballet classes. He would say, why are you wasting money on exercising?

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: By the time, I went to college I had accepted how things were between us. I tried not to tell him anything I cared about because I didn't think he really cared to listen. He didn't really want to know me. But we always stayed in touch, even though it was pretty surface. I would call him, check in.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Then, in 2021, my dad sunk into a deep depression. He was in such a dark place my older sister Kristel called me. She's in Ohio. I'm all the way in LA. She didn't know what to do.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I felt for my father. So I made him a part of my daily routine. I would call him every morning to remind him someone was thinking of him.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: In January of 2022, I call my father three times and he doesn't respond. Wednesday, nothing. Saturday, I leave a message. Monday, I leave another message.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Just as I'm putting my phone down, he calls me back. Hello? Dad? His voice is scratchy and dry. I can barely hear what he's saying. He's calling me from the floor.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: What do you mean you're on the floor? He fell. He's been on the floor for five days. I'm panicking. I keep my dad on my phone while I call Kristel with my boyfriend's phone. She says she's rushing over and hangs up.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: On the line with my dad, I keep him talking. I listen closely to his breathing. Then I hear everything unfold.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Through his phone, I hear my sister come into his apartment. I hear her call 911. I hear medics rush through the door. They ask my father a few questions.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: What's his name? Where does he live? How old is he?

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I hear a stretcher unfold. My sister picks up his phone and tells me she'll call me right back. Click.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I call my sister and ask for updates every day. The doctors don't know why my father fell. They don't know if he had a heart attack or a stroke. My sister tells me he's barely awake. He's having a hard time talking, walking, and going to the bathroom.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: After my dad is discharged from the hospital and checked into a rehabilitation facility, I buy a one-way plane ticket. I'm on my way back to my hometown in Ohio. My dad is 75, but when I see him for the first time after his fall, he looks like he's 90. Usually, he's a round, big belly guy. But now his skin is hanging off his face.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: His eyes are sunken in. His hair is unrecognizably long. And he has a beard. I didn't even know he could grow a beard.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Beside him is a walker. I quickly kiss him on the cheek and say, "Hi, Dad," pretending to be unfazed. I'm coming in all smiles. I'm the youngest in my family, you know, the one who makes the jokes, who intentionally brings an upbeat Kimmi Schmidt, Ted Lasso can-do spirit to family gatherings.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I kind of thought when I touched down in Ohio I would be the sunshine that saves my family. I would swoop in, relieve my sister, help my dad bounce back to himself, and then be back on an airplane. My dad spends a couple of weeks at the rehabilitation facility and then moves back home to his apartment.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I start living with him temporarily. I get him into a routine. And every morning, I have him do an exercise he loathes.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: OK, smile three times. Ready? One. Nice, OK, rest. All right, two. Big teeth, big teeth, there you go. OK, three, mm. Big, big, big, cheese, cheese, cheese. Beautiful. Smiling looks good on you, Dad.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I want his grin to remind him of the person he used to be, the person who moved across the world, Singapore to the US, as a 22 year old, totally alone to pursue a dream to attend college and study art. My father loved to draw. He made his living drawing and drafting streets at a civil engineering firm.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When we were all sleeping, he'd sketch cartoons and figures on old newspapers. I'd find them in the kitchen the next morning all over the metro section. After my dad retired, he would fly home to Singapore by himself to see his family. He would cook incredible Chinese food, fill his sketchbooks with portraits, and he was always in the middle of some big biography.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I want to say, Dad, that's who you are and that's who you can be again. But he fights me. He says, "no" and "I can't." This becomes his default response to everything. I feel like he's the boulder and I'm Sisyphus.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's weird to be in my hometown for more than three days. Usually, I'm in and I'm gone. As I accompany my sister and my dad to visit doctor after doctor, I feel like I'm getting a peek into their life together.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Kristel is 10 years older than me. When my parents got a divorce and sold our childhood home, she helped them sell it. She helped my father move into his apartment, connected him to his doctor when he needed one. For most of our lives, Kristel has been the one shouldering the family responsibilities I've always avoided.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: At one appointment, we visit my father's psychiatric nurse practitioner. After the three of us settle into her office, she directs her focus on my father. She asks him some intimate questions about his health and how he's been feeling, his mood, his motivation.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He answers honestly. He tells her he has nothing to live for, that there's no purpose in his life anymore, and that he feels lonely and isolated. I sit quietly and sink into the chair. My father would never say this to us directly, which is why I'm hearing it all for the first time.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A few minutes go by. And then the nurse turns to us. Because of his weakness, poor balance, cloudy thinking, and general fatigue, he can't live alone anymore, she says. She asks if he agrees. He does. But he tells her he feels guilty about burdening us. She looks at us again, smiles, and says one more thing, he should probably move in with one of you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Kristel and I talk it through. Dad could move in with her. But, to be honest, I don't know if that's such a good idea. She has a kid, multiple jobs. Her life is already so full, so stressful.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But in LA, my apartment is on the first floor. I have a walk-in shower, all the things he needs. I could do it. On my own, I decide, it has to be me. It just does.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Instead of seeing this moment as a burden, I want to see it as an opportunity. My father and I could become closer if we live together. But I need him to want this too. So at a family meeting, I put living in LA on the table to see what he says.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Two big questions, stay in Ohio or move to California. It's like choose your own adventure.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Based on my health basis, I don't think I can do either one.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: That's not a part of--

segments.speaker: Kristel
segments.text: That's not an option, Dad.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Yeah, and if you come to California, you would be staying with me. You say, me and Megan, new roommate situation, [LAUGHS] OK? If you stay in Ohio, you would be either in a retirement facility--

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Oh yeah?

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's clear my dad doesn't want to commit to anything. After 10 minutes of circling around a decision, I start to get impatient. I asked my father pointedly--

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: If I said, you have to move to California and live with me, how would you feel about that?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: I feel great.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Oh, oh, great.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: OK. All done.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: OK, great, let's choose that one. You said you'll feel great?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: I like California.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I do too.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: But--

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: No, no, no, I like this. Da-da-da-da.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Logistics.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Oh, Dad, logistics are logistics.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We're in Ohio for another three weeks. Now that we're counting down the days, my father's anxiety is ramping up. He doesn't understand how he's going to get on the plane or how we're going to get out of his apartment lease. He doesn't think he has enough pants for California. Everything is impossible.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: What's our deal? To have hope. Can you have hope? Say yes. Can you have hope? Say yes. Yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's hard for me to listen to this. I sound forceful, like a sunshine bully. My dad tries to say something, but I quickly interrupt him.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: [MUMBLING]

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Is this negative energy? What do you have to have? What do you have to have? Hope. Can you have hope?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Here we go again.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Yeah. We're going to live together.

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: How?

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Step by step. We're going to make it work, OK? I need you to trust me. Remember?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yes, trust me, your 31-year-old daughter, who has never been a caretaker before and is taking you away from everything you know.

segments.speaker: Flight Attendant
segments.text: Good morning and welcome aboard. Your flight crew this morning is Captain Oscar--

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Before this, I lived alone for three years. Then my boyfriend moved in and now my dad. There are three of us in my one bedroom apartment. When we walk in, I immediately start dad-proofing the rooms. I roll up all of my colorful rugs so my dad doesn't slip and fall. In my bathroom, I install a raised toilet seat and grip bars.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I give my father my bed and my bedroom. My boyfriend and I get the pullout bed in our dining room/office. I hide all my lingerie and sexy bathing suits.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: When my father lands in Los Angeles, he's still incredibly weak. And I'm not just his daughter. I'm also his secretary. I find him doctors and book his appointments. When he needs to pay a bill, we pay it together.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I'm also his nurse. I help him change his clothes and take showers. When he has an accident, I clean up the floors. He's having a hard time eating and I'm watching him lose weight. I monitor his appetite and cook him specific meals for breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I've brought in a crew of people to help. There's a speech, physical, and occupational therapists and a nurse who all come to visit. An hour here, an hour there. But I'm the first person he sees in the morning and the last person he sees at night. The weight of his moment-to-moment life is fully on my shoulders and I had no idea how heavy it would be.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: He can't sit down without my help, can't take a shower without me there. Every move he makes, I'm right beside him, his shadow. Still, I try to resume my life, launch back into work, make plans with friends, go out to bars. I try to take my dog to the park, cook and clean the house like usual.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: But it's just not possible. I cancel on my friends last minute. I can't keep the house clean. And I'm constantly running late to meetings. His life is my life. It's all consuming.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: But I can't tell my father that. We're together all the time. But I feel like I'm living this part of our life alone. And it's only been two weeks.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I need my dad to depend on me a little less or start to move in that direction. So I try to help him. At the kitchen table, I surround us with post-it notes and colorful markers, ready to brainstorm.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: If you can have anything, what do you want it to be?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I'm definitely more into this future planning than he is. He's closing his eyes and starting to fall asleep.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: Dad?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: How can you answer that question?

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: How can you answer that question?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: I don't know. Just make a goal.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: My dad once told me before I go to bed, I should envision the things I want to accomplish, that he used to do that. That's how he came to America. And that's always worked for me. But I can't convince him to make any goals. So I pick up a marker and start doing it for him.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan
segments.text: You want to become independent?

segments.speaker: Vincent
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Megan Tan

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: A school principal is a pretty classic "you're it" job. It's all you. When the school needs new math books, a new curriculum, a new budget, you're it. segments.text: I was called a fucking cunt. I was told to sit and spin on a sandpaper dildo. I was told to disappear. I was told to eat the end of a shotgun.

segments.speaker: Teresa Hill
segments.text: I was told not to go out in public. I was told, we're not coming to the school, we're coming to your house. And I lived in fear for four months after that.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: A friend of mine, an assistant principal for decades now, told me he still remembers his mentor explaining early on that the job of a school leader is never inflict pain on an institution. The job is to absorb pain for the institution. It must be confusing to be any kind of public official right now, trying to absorb the pain of the last few years.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How many principals or election officials or public health officials or prime ministers of countries have scrambled to respond to a public that is rageful by doing what they know how to do, by throwing PowerPoints at people, by holding public hearings, printing out color charts, only to finally understand that all the vitriol and misinformation was always going to be too enormous for any one person to absorb. Principal Hill shielded everyone else from distress until it was only hers.

segments.speaker: Teresa Hill
segments.text: But it wasn't just the words. It was the isolation that I felt with it. I felt like I was all alone in dealing with the situation. That is what made me say, I can't do this anymore.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So many of these voicemails are asking for you to resign.

segments.speaker: Teresa Hill
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So then when you did, did it feel like, oh, I don't want to give them what they wanted?

segments.speaker: Teresa Hill
segments.text: Of course. Of course. But I had to really dig deep and do what was best for me.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What was best for her was the one choice that was completely out of character, something far from her principalness and all her familiar moves. She decided not to be "it" anymore.
